issues.legal_issue: A transferee of property involved in a pending suit may be joined as a party when disputed questions about the transfer and the transferee’s interest must be resolved to adjudicate the suit completely and joining the transferee can avoid multiplicity of proceedings.
material_facts: A plaintiff sued her sons for maintenance and a charge over family property and obtained an order, based on counsel’s stated consent, restraining transfers during the suit.
One son subsequently sold shares in the disputed property to three purchasers, who sought to be joined as defendants and claimed to have paid consideration and received possession in good faith.
It was disputed whether the son had been a party to or knew of the restraint order, and the son alleged that the order had been procured fraudulently.
Proceedings concerning alleged disobedience of the order were pending, and the purchasers’ good-faith claims and the effect of the sales had not been resolved.
The court found that dismissing the purchasers’ joinder application without resolving those matters could lead them to bring a separate suit.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers were proper parties to the suit, and the order allowing their impleadment was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Order I, Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure empowers a court to add a person whose presence is necessary for effective and complete adjudication of the questions in the suit; avoiding multiplicity of proceedings is a relevant purpose. Khernchand Shankar Choudhari v. Vishnu Hari Patil recognizes that a transferee pendente lite may seek joinder and a hearing. Ramesh Hirachand Kundanmal v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay explains that joinder is a matter of judicial discretion, that the person must have a direct interest, and that joinder can avoid multiple actions. Surjit Singh v. Harbans Singh was distinguishable because there the parties’ knowledge of the restraint order was undisputed, whereas here the effect of the order and the transferees’ claims required determination.

rule.if: pending_property_suit and post_filing_transfer_of_suit_property and (binding_effect_of_restraining_order_is_disputed or transferee_good_faith_is_disputed) and transferee_has_direct_interest and (transferee_presence_needed_for_complete_adjudication or refusal_may_cause_separate_suit)

predicates.pending_property_suit: A claimant has brought a suit concerning rights in property, and that suit remains pending.
predicates.post_filing_transfer_of_suit_property: A party to the pending suit transferred an interest in the property involved in the suit after it was filed.
predicates.binding_effect_of_restraining_order_is_d: The parties dispute whether the transferor was bound by or knew of a court order restraining transfers of the property.
predicates.transferee_good_faith_is_disputed: The parties dispute whether the transferee acquired the interest in good faith for value.
predicates.transferee_has_direct_interest: The transferee claims an interest in the property that is the subject of the pending suit.
predicates.transferee_presence_needed_for_complete_: The transferee’s presence is needed to resolve the questions concerning the property and the claimed transfer effectively and completely.
predicates.refusal_may_cause_separate_suit: Excluding the transferee may lead the transferee to bring separate proceedings to enforce the claimed interest.
predicates.transferee_may_be_joined_as_party: The transferee may be added as a party to the pending suit.

issues.definition: When a transferee claims a direct interest in property in a pending suit, disputed transfer-related questions require resolution, and joinder is needed for complete adjudication or may avoid a separate suit, the transferee may be joined.

issues.legal_issue: Judicial officers who decided civil proceedings should not be named as parties merely because their orders are challenged in a writ petition or special leave petition.
material_facts: The judicial officers who had decided matters in the civil proceedings were named as respondents in the writ petition and the special leave petition challenging those proceedings.
The judgment found no necessity or justification for joining those officers as parties.
issues.conclusion: The court deprecated the practice and stated that judicial officers who dispose of civil proceedings should not be impleaded as parties in such writ petitions or special leave petitions.
issues.legal_principle: A judicial officer who decides a civil proceeding is not to be treated as a government official for the purpose of naming parties to a challenge to the proceeding. The court referred to writ petitions under Article 226 and special leave petitions under Article 138 of the Constitution of India in condemning the practice.

predicates.challenge_to_civil_proceeding_order: A litigant brings a writ petition or special leave petition challenging an order made in a civil proceeding.
predicates.judicial_officers_named_only_because_the: The judicial officers are made parties solely because they decided the civil proceeding being challenged.
predicates.judicial_officers_should_not_be_joined_a: The judicial officers should not be impleaded as parties to the challenge.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns an order in a civil proceeding and the deciding judicial officers are named only because they made that order, they should not be joined as parties.
